Theme 094 · Camera & edit grammar

Match Cut

A graphic-match film: every beat hands off to the next through one shared shape in the same spot of the frame, from a Friday-evening clock face to the Acme mark, to the coral anomaly dot, to the full stop of the tagline. Onion-skin ghosts, registration marks and an A ▸ B cut strip make each rhyme readable in a still.

1 · HOOK0:00–0:08

The minute hand ticks to 17:58 first, then the headline sets in word by word from the top line down; the clock face is framed dead centre so the cut can land on it. “Friday.” lands on the last beat before the drop.

The anomaly dot cuts to the full stop of the tagline, which types in around it; “Start free” scales up from 0.9 on beat 3. The last frame rhymes with the first.

COMPONENT KIT

  • Rhyme shape — one coral circle that survives every cut (clock face → mark dot → data point → full stop)
  • Onion-skin ghost — dashed outline of the previous shot so the still shows what it matched from
  • Registration marks — coral crosshair ticks locking the shared centre and diameter
  • A ▸ B cut strip — dark filmstrip band with the two thumbnails and a one-line “match on …” caption
  • Anomaly card — white card carrying the −18% line and the Roll back / Acknowledge choice
  • Dotted headline — tagline whose full stop is the coral dot, so the last rhyme is the CTA

MOTION · MUSIC

  • Hard graphic cut — 0-frame cut, placed exactly on a downbeat (the drop at 0:08 and bar lines after it); shape centre and size identical on both sides of the cut
  • Push-in to the rhyme — scale 1 → 1.35 over 1 bar (2 s at 120 BPM) with power2.in into the shape, so the cut happens at peak motion
  • Settle after the cut — the incoming shot eases out from 1.08 → 1 in 0.5 s (expo.out) while secondary text staggers in at 0.25 s, one item per eighth note

WHY / RISK · ADAPT IT

Match cuts make separate ideas feel like one thought: the clock, the product, the data and the promise become the same object. It needs almost no production, only very precise layout. Risk: if positions drift by even a few pixels the rhyme reads as a glitch, and more than four rhymes turn into a trick.

Adapt to your product: Find one shape your product already owns (an avatar circle, a status dot, a card corner, a cursor) and plan every scene so that shape sits at the same place in the frame at each cut. Build the shots around the rhyme, not the other way round.

References: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Match_cut (match cut definition; 2001 bone-to-satellite and North by Northwest examples) · https://www.studiobinder.com/blog/1917-one-shot-cinematography/ (hidden match cuts used to stitch long takes)
